newsitem.title: KENYA: Kabila's Congo shifts Africa's political alliances.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo shifts Africa's political alliances.

text.p: Victory by Laurent Kabila in the Democratic Republic of Congo -- formerly Zaire and Africa's third largest country -- has shattered old political alliances and redrawn the military equation in East and Central Africa.

Kabila's Rwandan-backed Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) took power last month after toppling the regime of Mobutu Sese Seko -- Africa's longest serving president.

The victory was cheered by Zaireans tired of the corruption and economic stagnation that characterised most of the Mobutu years. But some of Zaire's neighbours were even happier to see the end of the regional leader who supported groups opposed to them.
According to regional analysts, political sources and diplomats, this is how countries have either benefitted from Kabila's victory or face dramatic upheavals as a result:
RWANDA: The immediate beneficiary of Kabila's victory was tiny and ethnically divided Rwanda which feared destabilisation from over a million Hutus exiled in Zaire.

Many Hutus fled their motherland in 1994 after the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Over half of them took refuge in Zaire from where leaders plotted a violent return to Rwanda. The failure to keep the refugees under control was the main reason for Rwanda's military intervention in Zaire.
By smashing Mobutu's regime, Rwanda and Kabila managed to eliminate, at least for the time being, any external threats to the Tutsi-controlled government in Rwanda.

BURUNDI: Kabila's rebellion began by closing refugee camps and rear bases inside Zaire used by Burundi's Hutu guerrillas to launch hit-and-run attacks. Burundi's support for Kabila helped ease the isolation of Pierre Buyoya's Tutsi-dominated military regime but the rebels are still active inside the tiny country and have some political support in neighbouring Tanzania.

ANGOLA: As soon as Kabila took office in ex-Zaire, neighbouring Angola lurched towards renewed civil war between the MPLA-dominated government and the former rebel group UNITA. A fragile peace process, bank-rolled by the United Nations and which ended 20 years of superpower-backed war, is at high risk.

The Angolan flareup is directly linked to the defeat of Mobutu, UNITA's principal ally. Jonas Savimbi's movement lost its supply lines and its vital diamond selling network in Zaire. Kabila has the staunch support of the Angolan government which some analysts believe hopes to crush UNITA's military capacity once and for all.

SUDAN: The Islamic-backed government in Khartoum was close to Mobutu and often used the northern part of Zaire to keep southern rebels in Sudan in check. The rebels of the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) are Kabila allies and Mobutu's exit has seen them regain control over vast areas of the south. Other pro-Kabila states, Ethiopian and Eritrea, are involved in the moves to force change in Khartoum, diplomats say.

UGANDA: The departure of Mobutu and the SPLA's victories have diminished the threat long posed by exiled Ugandan rebel groups who freely operated from eastern Zaire and southern Sudan. President Yoweri Museveni is Kabila's political godfather, according to many analysts.

CONGO: The upheaval and vicious militia battles in the Republic of Congo, ex-Zaire's small neighbour, is directly linked to events in Zaire. The fighting exploded in Brazzaville days after Kabila took office across the river in Kinshasa where the new Alliance government has not hidden its dislike for President Pascal Lissouba. He is blamed for staying too close to Mobutu until the end. There are strong indications that both Kabila and Angola have given their political support -- at the very least -- to Lissouba's foe and presidential predecessor, Denis Sassou-Nguesso. The arrival in Congo of around 20,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, some of them armed, is likely to further destabilise the Congo.

CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: This politically unstable country could also fall victim to the post-Mobutu shake-up, analysts say. Armed members of Mobutu's defeated army and presidential guard have crossed into the Central African Republic and Kabila will be anxious to neutralise the potential threat from them. The country is also the pivot of France's military presence in Africa, another factor which Kabila and his regional supporters are taking into account.
